#10282. Delta’s free Wi-Fi was just the beginning. The airline has bigger plans with T-Mobile

Free in-flight Wi-Fi is nice. So is a complimentary cocktail at 35,000 feet. But Delta and T-Mobile aren’t done finding ways to make their customers happy.

The two companies have spent the past few years building a partnership that gives travelers a few extra reasons to choose Delta and T-Mobile. Now, with the launch of T-Mobile’s new T-Mix wireless plans, they’re already thinking about what might come next.

In an interview with Fast Company, Ranjan Goswami, Delta’s chief marketing officer, and Mike Belcher, T-Mobile’s senior vice president of business development, partnerships and loyalty programs, confirmed that they’re exploring additional perks, including potentially expanding Delta’s offerings beyond SkyMiles.

“We started with Miles, but what else can we do together?” Goswami said. “What do T-Mobile customers want?”

Neither executive was ready to share specifics, but both made it clear that the companies have more ideas in the works.

T-Mobile’s new plans could mean more Delta perks

Announced in October, T-Mix takes a different approach to wireless plans. Instead of giving everyone the same collection of benefits, T-Mobile is letting customers pick the perks they’ll actually use.

The plans, which launch in November, come in three tiers: Standard, More, and Loaded. Prices start at $55, $75, and $95 per month for a single line, respectively, with AutoPay, plus taxes and fees.

Depending on their plan, customers can select between one and three benefits through a feature called Picks. Options include subscriptions and perks from companies such as Netflix, Apple Music, DoorDash, YouTube Premium, and Delta Air Lines.

For frequent travelers, one of those choices is Delta SkyMiles, giving eligible T-Mobile customers another way to earn airline rewards.

Customers can also switch up many of their selections during designated windows throughout the year, so they’re not necessarily stuck with the same perks forever.

And Delta might eventually offer more than just miles.

“You know, I would hope that our offering in T-Mix is even more broad,” Goswami told Fast Company when asked what the partnership might look like three years from now.

“I think there’s so much space to experiment there because T-Mobile’s built a platform that allows us to put so many choices in front of customers, and we’re excited to kind of be a part of that journey,” Goswami said.

Belcher said customer feedback will play a big role in determining what gets added next. T-Mobile is already gathering suggestions from customers and frontline employees, and those ideas could help shape future offerings.

“And so, you know, if we get other ideas from customers on what they want to see between Delta and T-Mobile, that’s something we’ll look at,” Belcher said.

For now, neither company has announced any specific new Delta perks or when they might arrive.

From free Wi-Fi to drinks and now airline miles

The Delta and T-Mobile partnership has come a long way since the companies first teamed up to bring free in-flight Wi-Fi to Delta passengers.

What started as a connectivity benefit has grown into something much bigger.

According to Goswami, Delta expects to surpass 115 million logins to its Delta Sync Wi-Fi service, powered by T-Mobile, this year. The service is now available on roughly 1,300 aircraft, including flights to the Asia Pacific region.

And passengers are doing a lot more than checking email. With free connectivity, travelers can stream entertainment, catch up on work, or follow live sporting events while they’re in the air.

The companies later added another benefit: a complimentary premium in-flight drink for eligible T-Mobile customers flying Delta.

Now, with SkyMiles available through T-Mix, the partnership is expanding beyond the flight itself.

“We added on drinks. Now we’re in T-Mix, and you know, watch this space. We’re working on more stuff,” Goswami said.

Belcher said the goal behind expanding the partnership is pretty straightforward.

“What influenced us to evolve it was to continue to deliver more value to our customers,” he said. And the conversations aren’t stopping with T-Mix.

“You know, we’re continuing to talk about other things that we can do across our ecosystem,” Belcher said.

Of course, those freebies also have a business benefit.

Goswami described how something as simple as a complimentary drink could get passengers talking. If someone sitting next to a T-Mobile customer sees them receive a free drink, they might start wondering what other perks they’re missing out on. That could make them more interested in switching wireless carriers. Likewise, a T-Mobile customer who starts earning Delta miles might be more inclined to book their next flight with the airline.

In other words, a free drink isn’t necessarily just a nice gesture. It can also be a pretty effective marketing tool.

Why Delta and T-Mobile want to keep expanding their partnership

The companies’ relationship is also part of a bigger shift in how brands think about customer loyalty.

These days, earning points or getting the occasional discount isn’t always enough to keep customers coming back. Companies are increasingly teaming up with brands outside their industries to offer benefits people can use in everyday life.

“I think partnerships are the future. No brand can be on their own,” Goswami said.

Delta already has relationships with American Express, Starbucks, and Uber, giving customers opportunities to earn rewards in places that have little to do with booking a flight.

T-Mobile has been doing something similar for years through T-Mobile Tuesdays, which offers customers weekly freebies, discounts, and other benefits.

Belcher explained that the company’s approach to loyalty is a little different from the traditional model. Rather than asking customers to prove how loyal they are to T-Mobile, the company wants to show customers why it’s worth sticking around.

“We flip the script on loyalty a little bit,” Belcher said. “We feel it’s T-Mobile’s job to show our loyalty to our customers.”

T-Mix takes that idea further by giving customers more say in which benefits they receive, rather than assuming everyone wants the same things. And for Delta, that creates an opportunity to reach customers who might not otherwise be thinking about the airline.

Neither company is saying exactly what the next benefit will be. But considering how quickly the partnership has grown from free Wi-Fi to cocktails and airline miles, there’s a good chance customers will have more to look forward to.

As Goswami put it, the companies are already working on more stuff.

This could help Ukrainian operatives see what Russian drone operators are seeing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

CODE380, a radio manufacturer based in Kyiv, just built a new software-defined radio (SDR) that intercepts analog video signals that Russian drones transmit to their operators, making it easier for troops to find and intercept them. According to Defense News, the D·Vision SDR can sweep radio frequencies from 500 MHz to 8.7 GHz and convert any intercepted analog radio signal into a video feed. It has a detection range of up to six miles for signals on the 540 MHz to 6 GHz band, and up to two to three miles for higher frequencies.

Although this isn’t the first passive Ukraine-made drone detector, it’s one of the lightest models produced so far, weighing just 10 ounces or 290 grams — by comparison, an iPhone 18 Pro Max weighs about 8.78 ounces or 249 grams. Its competitors include the Vydun 7.5, which weighs around 2 pounds or 900 grams and could intercept signals at up to 7.5 GHz; the 23-ounce (650-gram) Chuyka 3.0, which can detect signals at up to 8.8 GHz; and the SENSE-4, which weighs 21 ounces or 600 grams and could detect drone signals of up to 8.2 GHz.

All these receivers cover the 4.1 to 4.5 GHz band that Russian Molniya strike drones began using in June of this year to transmit video back to their operators, Presidential advisor Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said. However, he also warned against relying on them for protection alone. “Most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly,” he said in a social media post. “I’m warning you so that trust in a detector doesn’t cost you your life.” These receivers are often designed to work in tandem with other sensors, like radar, acoustic sensors, and drone interceptors, as part of an anti-drone defense system.

Most of these units are designed to intercept analog signals, meaning they won't be useful for intercepting video signals once Russia figures out how to use digital signals. Still, the D·Vision SDR is claimed to have digital UAV detection, although it’s only tuned towards DJI drones for now. It’s unclear what types of radios Russian drones use, though, so the company would have to recover downed units to inspect their hardware and build appropriate countermeasures. It will also be ineffective against fiber optic drones, which are both jam- and intercept-proof as they use a physical connection to communicate with their home base.

#10279. Elon Musk says Tesla will refund many Cybertruck orders for this unconventional reason

Elon Musk has had a rough week. His nearly half a billion dollars in midterm election spending on Republican candidates went to waste as a blue tsunami swept the nation. Stocks for his companies Tesla and SpaceX fell in the wake of the election. And to top it off, Musk announced that Tesla would be “winding down” production of its infamous Cybertrucks by the middle of 2027.

Now Musk has added another layer to the Cybertruck’s discontinuation scenario: It will require Tesla to issue refunds to “a lot of people” who’ve ordered the vehicle and won’t receive one.

In a post on X, Musk wrote that shutting down Cybertruck production has little to do with the sci-fi-inspired truck’s profits (or lack thereof). Rather, he claimed, it’s a shift to prioritize the brand’s newest vehicle, the autonomous Cybercab.

“The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate,” Musk wrote. “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

He added: “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.”

Though Musk alleged that the Cybertruck’s profits have been misrepresented in the media, its sales numbers tell a different story. According to data from Kelley Blue Book, sales for the Cybertruck have declined since 2024. Only 16,000 of the vehicles have been shipped so far in 2026, a far cry from Musk’s prelaunch estimate that Tesla would be manufacturing 250,000 Cybertrucks per year.

The announcement continues a trend for Tesla, which also discontinued its Model S and X electric vehicles at the beginning of 2026. At the time, Musk said the decision was to free up Tesla’s resources to focus on other products—in that case, its bipedal Optimus robot, which has yet to hit the market.

On Tesla’s Q4 2025 earnings call, Musk said it was time to give the EVs “an honorable discharge” as Tesla entered a new era, adding, “We’re really moving into a future that is based on autonomy.”

It’s slow, it’s loud, but it runs on old Optane.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A homelab builder on Reddit has run Moonshot AI’s 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 AI model on discontinued second-gen Optane PMem 200 memory, using a 40-core 3rd-gen Xeon Scalable CPU and not a GPU for inference. The build runs hot, and the builder’s advice is that you “treat active DIMM cooling as mandatory,” with dual 12W blower fans aimed at the modules to get temperatures under control. The project, a follow-up to a separate user’s first-gen Optane build earlier this year, runs at a sluggish 0.85 tokens per second even with 1-bit quantization.

Kimi K3 is absolutely not built for home use, in our estimation, with Moonshot AI recommending data center inference engines to run it, and even the smallest community quantization needs at least 610GB of RAM. Using secondhand Optane, instead, is one of the few ways to reach that capacity at home. It doesn’t help that DRAM prices have skyrocketed, and the builder says the Optane memory costs “a fraction” of the equivalent.

Intel launched its Optane Persistent Memory 200 Series (PMem 200) in 2020 for its 3rd-gen Xeon Scalable CPUs in 128GB, 256GB, and 512GB capacities. On two-socket Xeon platforms, it runs at a higher effective MT/s rate than the first generation (PMem 100) that was used on the first project, and it can deliver an average of up to 32% more memory bandwidth. Optane can run in either Memory Mode or App Direct Mode; both builds had platforms allowing for each.

Memory Mode has the Optane act as system memory with DRAM as its cache, the method used in the first build, while App Direct exposes Optane as a separate, persistent region that the software maps directly, the mode used in the second. This can give “more control over where the model’s tensors live,” according to the first build’s creator, u/APFrisco, who planned to try it.

Performance does take a hit by going with Optane over DRAM, and with the higher 3-bit quantization, the speed went down even more to 0.75 tokens per second. One commenter points out that this is very slow, with a 50k-token task estimated to take 13 hours at about 1 token per second, but another notes that overnight batches don’t care as much about speed. Both speeds compare to the first build’s roughly 4 tokens per second, although in that case the builder had an RTX 3060 handling part of the model in addition to Memory Mode, a 2-bit quantization, and the smaller, earlier 1-trillion-parameter K2.5 model.

The latest builder also had to deal with heat output, with the Optane DIMMs getting “extremely hot” with sustained inference, creating a situation the builder says can endanger neighboring DRAM. That heat is consistent with Intel’s own specs, as the manufacturer rates the modules with forced airflow of 2.4 to 2.7 meters per second for cooling, which is what you expect to find in data centers. You might not normally have this level of airflow pointed directly at your memory sticks.

The expected operating conditions put each Optane module at 12W or 15W, regardless of capacity. If the build used four sticks, that would mean up to 60W of heat placed right next to the system memory. Throttling on these occurs at 83 degrees Celsius, with a thermal trip shutdown at 85 degrees, compared to the 85 degrees Celsius and up to 95 degrees in an extended range that typical DDR4 server memory is rated for. A lot of heat has to be removed from the system to keep things running.

The performance numbers given are pre-tuning — this means without tuning thread counts or NUMA affinity — so there is room for improvement, and one commenter also asked about using Memory Mode with DRAM caching for the most-used experts. The builder plans to add GPUs and to also load parts of the model into DRAM as a faster tier alongside the Optane, with “more benchmarks to come.”

#10277. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.

#10275. Oppo confirms its next foldable will actually know what a ‘global’ release is

The Oppo Find N6 is a stunning foldable but, for the second year in a row, it really stretches the definition of what a “global” release means. Oppo Find N7, apparently, will fix that.

Oppo Find N5 and Find N6 both saw global launches, but the company’s definition of that excluded Europe and virtually every other major market. For the most part, both foldables were essentially sold only in China, with major markets elsewhere left out. And that’s a shame, because both raised the bar for foldables in major ways.

Now, we’re looking forward to the launch of Oppo Find N7, a device rumored to be adopting the wide form factor popularized by Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, and that Oppo technically offered before anyone else.

And it might actually get a global release.

Speaking to Nixanbal (via GSMArena), Oppo apparently confirmed that its next foldable will see a release in Europe. It’d be the first time an Oppo foldable made its way to the region, with the OnePlus Open serving as Oppo’s global foldable back in 2023 for its one and only generation.

As for a release date, that’s still unconfirmed, but Oppo tends to release new foldables early in the year, so March 2027, give or take, is probably when we’ll see more officially.

#10274. Americans are sacrificing to afford holiday gifts this year. Here’s how

Visa released its 2026 Holiday Spending Outlook report, and it found that while consumers put travel at the top of their holiday shopping list, they plan to spend the bulk of their money this season on gifts.

The survey also found a real difference in who is traveling, and in overall holiday spending based on income levels, as Americans face high inflation and an increasing cost of living.

More than half of those surveyed say they’d prefer to travel and go to live events—but only 15% are actually pulling the trigger on experiences. Meanwhile, 27% plan to buy physical gifts, according to Visa, the top payment network in the U.S.

This is partly because of the high cost of travel—made worse by soaring fuel prices and the war in Iran—which has many Americans sticking closer to home for the holidays. Those unused travel dollars could flow into merchandise instead, which is good news for retailers, according to Visa’s economists.

The only exception to the rule is households earning an income of $200,000 and up: They increased both holiday airfare bookings and spending in September, with bookings up 29% and spending up 38%.

In contrast, roughly 33% of consumers earning under $100,000 plan to switch to lower-cost brands or budget-friendly stores for gifts, indicating how these shoppers are adapting to higher prices, Visa said.

Overall, Visa’s Business and Economic Insights (VBEI) team forecasts U.S. holiday retail sales will rise 4.5% year over year in November and December, the strongest growth since 2021. (However, that figure is in part due to inflation. Without taking price increases into consideration, sales are expected to increase 1.1%, down from 1.3% last year.)

Individuals are planning to spend an average of $777 on gifts this year, signaling Americans’ continued willingness to open their wallets, even as shoppers look for value in the face of inflation.

“Consumers are heading into the holidays with the capacity and willingness to spend, even if they’re being thoughtful about where those dollars go,” Michael Brown, principal U.S. economist at Visa, said in a statement. “Income growth continues to provide an important foundation for spending, and while higher prices remain part of the picture, we expect another healthy holiday season.”

Visa surveyed 4,660 U.S. adults 18 and older to get a sense of the broader consumer sentiment.

#10272. I bought the knock-off Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air bands, and it’s crazy how good they are [Gallery]

I love swapping out the bands on my Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air, but Google’s official options are not cheap. It doesn’t take long to find a plethora of knock-off Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air bands around the web and, as it turns out, they’re actually really good.

Over the past few generations, I’ve collected a ton of Pixel Watch bands and, at first, that was almost entirely first-party bands. For the first couple of years of Pixel Watch, third-party bands were either non-existent or of terrible quality, but they’ve gotten a lot better.

Last year, I showcased some knock-off Active Sport bands that, for $8, very effectively filled the gap for me while Google’s lineup was lacking some colors I wanted.

Since then, I’ve tried others. The most recent batch is a 6-pack of Pixel Watch bands that are copies of Google’s standard “Active” band. They’re made from silicone, not the fluorelastomer from past generations, nor the “Hydrogenated Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (HNBR)” used on Pixel Watch 5. But, in action, it gets the job done.

The bands sit somewhere between Google’s small and large sizes and slot into the Pixel Watch 5’s mechanism perfectly. If you handed this to me and said it was an official band from Google, I’d probably believe you.

To get this level of quality at such a low price is wild, all while getting colors that, again, Google doesn’t make. I found this while just wanting a purple band, but the price tag pushed me to just buy a whole pack, and the striking deep red included sneakily became one of my favorites.

Pixel Watch isn’t alone here – third-party knock-off bands for Fitbit Air are very good, as my colleage Damien Wilde has pointed out repeatedly.

I originally bought the Stephen Curry edition Fitbit Air and, long story short, I don’t have that official band anymore. But the $9 (currently even cheaper!) knock-off I bought on Amazon is quite literally identical in quality, feel, and even the details. The only thing it’s missing is the Stephen Curry badge (which, frankly, I don’t miss anyway), but it still has that little piece of added material where the wordmark would have been.

The same goes for the matching band I picked up for my Pixel Watch 5.

Google doesn’t sell this band on its own, which is annoying, but the knock-off I bought is basically identical to what I felt during our hands-on with the official one back in August, though this one doesn’t have the space for the Stephen Curry badge the real one does. The lugs connecting to the watch are also different and not nearly as stylish, but I’m absolutely not complaining here.

Is it possible that Google’s supply chain is producing these near-identical versions? Given the quality at play, I really wouldn’t be surprised! That said, a lot of these are simple copies. It’s not all that hard to spin up generic versions of products like these.

Most third party cheap Fitbit Air bands I've tried range from "decent" to "very good".

Most third party cheap and expensive Pixel Watch bands I've tried range from "very, very bad" to "almost decent".

The major issue with PW 3rd party bands isn't the band itself. It's the connecting lugs.

Not how they look, but how they're manufactured. High tolerances, rattling, too lose or too tight connections.

And that applies also to certified "made for Google" bands (i.e. the Spigen ones).

I've given up. I'm going to buy the official Pixel Watch leather band and take the official lugs out of it, so I can use with any 22mm strap.

I’ll still happily pick up some of Google’s official bands because it’s hard to beat some of those color options but, for the most part, it’s getting hard to go wrong with the knock-off Pixel Watch bands, and even more so with the Fitbit Air. The simpler tracker gets even better third-party options seeing as Google made the mounting mechanism free for everyone.

Whatever the case, third-party / knock-off Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air bands are in a really good place right now, and that’s refreshing after a few years of using this lineup every day.

The latest CPU-Z hardware survey data shows 32GB and 64GB memory configurations down 2.5% and 18% year on year, respectively. The driving factor is no mystery: High-capacity memory has become a luxury in modern PC builds. The AI rush is still gobbling up the global DRAM supply, so prices for the best RAM options across DDR4 and DDR5 have gone through the roof.

If you are not familiar with CPU-Z, it is a free program that gives you a detailed breakdown of the hardware inside your system. It only tracks systems where it is actually installed and running, so it does not report monthly retail sales figures. Do not take the data as sales figures in any sense. They represent CPU-Z's active user base.

32GB and 16GB are common configurations that have grown over the years. According to the gathered data, 32GB configurations lead CPU-Z's user base with a 37.2% share, with 16GB configurations close behind at 33%. Not a surprise, really, since applications and games have grown more memory-intensive. 16GB has been the baseline for a long time now, and 32GB is now the sweet spot for many people, even gamers.

On the flip side, 8GB configurations have been steadily declining. They make up only 11% of the surveyed systems. 8GB systems are rare nowadays. You may still find them in legacy systems, basic office machines, or extremely budget-limited builds where performance takes a backseat. Meanwhile, higher-end configurations, including 64GB and 24GB, are still in the minority at 7.3% and 2.3%, respectively.

Fresh stats from CPU-Z! 🔎 For the first time ever, RAM capacity on PCs has declined year-over-year : -2.5% for 32 GB and -18% for 64 GB! https://t.co/ya0soA55bRNovember 6, 2026

For the first time, the CPU-Z developer recorded a noticeable decline in higher-capacity configurations. Specifically, 32GB configurations fell 2.5% year over year, while 64GB options dropped a significant 18%. This is likely due to the steep rise in memory prices, which has forced consumers to reconsider the cost-benefit of larger capacities.

As the price per gigabyte goes up, buyers are opting for more affordable capacities. Lower-capacity memory kits have seen a somewhat revival. The 16GB configuration, often considered the minimum, has rebounded by 12.9%. Similarly, 8GB configurations, which were previously in sharp decline, grew 5.5%.

Interestingly, 24GB configurations also increased by 19.7% and have become a compromise for consumers who need more than 16GB of memory but do not want to spend a lot of money on a premium 32GB memory kit.

The current distribution between DDR4 and DDR5 memory types reveals that DDR4 remains the dominant memory standard at 54.5%. In contrast, DDR5, despite being the latest memory technology, is still in its early adoption phase at 32.9%. DDR4 has been the de facto standard for almost a decade now, so it will take time for DDR5 to overtake it.

Nonetheless, the noticeable 6% growth in DDR4 and 2.9% decline in DDR5 suggests budget-conscious consumers are sticking with platforms that still embrace DDR4, such as AMD's Zen 3-powered Ryzen 5000 (codenamed Vermeer) or Intel's 13th Generation Raptor Lake processors. CPU-Z's processor charts show a significant increase in Zen 3 chips, including the Ryzen 7 5700X, Ryzen 5 5600, and Ryzen 5 5500, with figures up to 42.8%, 36.1%, and 67.3%, respectively.

Although both DDR4 and DDR5 have increased in price, the former remains slightly more affordable. Companies are supporting the effort too, such as AMD rereleasing the Ryzen 7 5800X3D, vendors restarting DDR4 and DDR4 motherboard production, or Intel preparing rewarmed Raptor Lake Next chips for 2027.

#10269. DC Studios shake-up: James Gunn and Peter Safran exit, Skydance appoints a Marvel veteran

Superman, Batman, and the rest of the DC heroes are getting a new boss, yet again.

Skydance Motion Picture Group announced Monday that James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-chief executives after four years leading DC Studios. Although their first film leading the superhero factory, Superman, reached theaters only last year, their DC run has come to an abrupt end.

Gunn and Safran initially survived Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The studio’s merger with Paramount Pictures was finalized just as DC’s Clayface was released.

However, it turns out Gunn and Safran aren’t surviving the merger. Instead, Skydance chairman and chief executive David Ellison is turning to Jeremy Latcham, a veteran of Marvel Studios, to steer DC.

“James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of,” Ellison said in a statement. “We’re grateful for their passion, contributions, and commitment to this legendary brand.”

Latcham was a leading executive for Marvel, including the first wave of the Marvel Cinematic Universe with Iron Man and The Avengers. He also worked with Gunn and Safran on Guardians of the Galaxy.

The changeover will take effect December 1. But a long pipeline of projects already in production ensures that Gunn and Safran’s fingerprints will be on DC Studios for a while to come. Gunn is currently in post-production on the Superman follow-up, Man of Tomorrow. Other upcoming releases include the series The People v. Gorilla Grodd and The Batman: Part II.

But the decade’s worth of planning that Gunn and Safran instituted will no longer come to fruition. Their reign has been characterized by more idiosyncratic comic book adaptations and genre gambles, like Clayface, which fused superhero with horror. (It’s grossed $109 million so far.) Earlier this year, Supergirl flopped, a major setback in just their second release.

Latcham takes on the roles of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. He will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

“Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” Goldberg and Greenstein said.

Gunn’s biggest success leading DC was Superman, which struck a decidedly different and more comedic tone than the previous treatments of the iconic hero in Zack Snyder’s Man of Steel. But it also didn’t reach the box-office heights of the biggest superhero hits, grossing $618.7 million worldwide.

From the start, Gunn, a prodigious filmmaker, was an unusual choice for such a prominent corporate leadership role. In exiting DC, he seemed eager to concentrate again on writing and directing.

“We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow,” Gunn and Safran said in a statement.

Latcham had been out of the superhero business. In 2017, he departed Marvel to set up Latcham Pictures, producing films including Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves and Bad Times at the El Royale.

“I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era,” Latcham said.

—By Jake Coyle, AP film writer

#10267. How to Use CSS Attribute Selectors to Build More Flexible User Interfaces

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them. According to The New York Times, these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.

This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication.

Many of these approved companies include well-known entities like Baidu, BYD, Tesla Shanghai, as well as ZTE, which has previously been blacklisted from the U.S. market, Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra. The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.

The New Matrix website also reportedly did not contain any information about its owners or its history, although public company records reveal that it was founded by Li Bin, who, along with two other primary owners, are connected to Wise Road, a Chinese private equity firm sanctioned by the U.S. for helping Beijing acquire sensitive chip technologies. Furthermore, Mr. Li chairs Tsinghua Unigroup, a tech conglomerate partly owned by the Chinese government, and owns New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, which has also been added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List for cooperating with the Chinese military.

Maginfra, on the other hand, is suspected of being linked to Inspur, which Washington has blacklisted since 2023 for supporting the People’s Liberation Army, with both companies sharing personnel, patents, and a similar government ownership structure. These two firms aren’t listed as the final users of Nvidia’s AI chips, though. Instead, they’re supposed to assemble them into AI servers, which would then be forwarded to a final user, although it’s unclear who their customers are.

Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links. Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology’s executives are reportedly related to the founder of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a data center operator that has sold compute capacity to Chinese military contractors. It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025, even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors. The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China. Beijing’s refusal to give Chinese tech companies the green light to buy the chips for the first few months of the year caused the delay. But once China lifted its import ban on Nvidia chips, several Chinese companies applied for licenses to buy them, and The New York Times reported that around two dozen firms have already received approval, including these questionable ones.

#10265. The midterms sent Washington a warning about housing. The numbers explain why

Americans have handed the new Congress its marching orders: Tackle the affordability crisis that’s keeping so many young people locked out of the housing market.

Housing affordability was one of several key themes that resonated with voters from South Carolina and Ohio to Texas, Montana, and beyond, helping more than 40 Democrats to flip seats in both the Senate and House of Representatives during last week’s midterm elections. Survey after survey pointed to young people, in particular, who feel downtrodden about the prospect of homeownership—and various indicators underscore why.

Earlier this year, the National Association of Realtors reported that the typical first-time homebuyer is now 40 years old, a record high and a sharp increase from even five years ago, when the age was 33. Meanwhile, surging home prices, especially in areas of the country where wages haven’t kept pace, have driven the share of first-time buyers to a record low of 21% last year and have barely budged since then, figures from the Chicago-based trade group show.

But voters will need to see that the new Democrat-controlled Congress is taking these issues seriously, or the party risks being ousted once again in 2028, veteran Democratic strategist Donna Brazile cautioned during a conference hosted by the National Association of Realtors over the weekend.

“Affordability, affordability, affordability. It’s not a slogan that Democrats can use again unless they do something about it,” Brazile said, as reported by Realtor.com. 

While Congress passed landmark legislation over the summer with the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that targeted boosting the supply of affordable housing, Wall Street also seems optimistic about the implications of a greater focus on affordability. A stock index made up of 34 companies in the homebuilding industry has risen nearly 4.2% since last Tuesday’s close. 

HOUSING AFFORDABILITY IN FOCUS 

While the housing market has eased in some ways in recent years, it’s not been enough to get many prospective homebuyers in the door of a new home.

The median price of a home on the market, at $415,000 as of October, has fallen nearly 8% from a high of $449,000 in June 2022, according to figures from Realtor.com. But mortgage rates have also risen in recent years, as the average 30-year mortgage rate surged from less than 3% in late 2020 to as high as 8% in late 2023, according to Mortgage News Daily. And rates are still relatively high, at 7.18% currently.

This year has seen the cost of nearly everything increase amid a surge in fuel prices stemming from the war in Iran. To tame inflation, the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark federal funds rate for the first time in more than three years in September—and traders broadly expect that central bankers will do so again in December, which means mortgage rates could remain higher. 

While many personal finance experts recommend that people spend no more than 30% of their pretax income on housing costs, many Americans are exceeding that limit. In fact, 29% of homeowners with a mortgage are spending more than this threshold on housing—marking the third consecutive year of gains, according to the latest data from the Census Bureau, as reported by Investopedia.

To deal with rising housing costs, 59% of renters and homeowners alike say they’re taking steps to manage—either finding additional work or tapping into savings, according to a survey conducted by Experian in September. And the housing market seems like such a lost cause that more than one-third of renters don’t think they’ll ever be able to afford a home despite wanting to, according to a quarterly survey conducted by CNBC and SurveyMonkey. 

With the election so squarely focused on the cost of living—and housing affordability—the new Congress has a directive when it convenes in January, as Ali Solis, CEO of Solis Strategic Solutions, told Affordable Housing Finance. 

“Voters sent a clear message that the cost of rent, homeownership being out of reach, and everyday living cost is way too high,” she said. “People are struggling, and they want Washington to act.”

#10262. Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang. But its board may have no interest in challenging its leader

While Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into bombshell reports that Chinese intelligence targeted CEO Jensen Huang—and that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy—early indications suggest that the company’s board may be unwilling or unable to challenge its rock star CEO.

On October 29, when The New York Times first reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concerns about Huang’s contacts with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed, the company characterized the relationship as an ordinary business matter and said it didn’t share classified information with customers.

The board did not announce an investigation until 10 days later, after Huang acknowledged the affair in a memo to staff, emphasizing that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” And before the investigation even started, the board had already said it had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

The announcement also framed the investigation as focused on national security, without mentioning whether it would address potential concerns about Huang’s judgment or conduct as an executive.

Nvidia has said Huang will continue serving as CEO without interruption.

Fast Company reached out to Nvidia for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Indeed, there may be little Nvidia’s board can do to punish Huang without seriously risking the company’s business, which has become inextricable from Huang himself.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has spent more than three decades transforming it from a maker of graphics chips into a dominant force in the artificial intelligence boom. The 63-year-old is involved in nearly every aspect of the company’s business—from product development to its relationships with customers and government officials—with more than 60 executives reporting directly to him.

That dependence could make the board’s task particularly difficult. Nvidia has no publicly identified successor to Huang, and analysts have warned that his departure could create enormous uncertainty for the company.

“Jensen is not replaceable,” wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at New Jersey-based financial firm Yorkville Ives & Co. “There is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO.”

After fashioning itself the party of Donald Trump, GOP leaders are beginning to slowly distance themselves from the president as the Democrats’ historic blowout wins in the midterm elections lay bare the fractures in the MAGA movement.

#10260. Electoral College on the chopping block: Democrats now have the power to end it. Will they?

Amid the excitement of the blue wave’s flashier victories in last week’s midterm elections—Blexas, Bliowa, and Blansas, anyone?—Democrats also quietly set themselves up for one of the biggest potential changes in the history of American politics: ending the Electoral College.

The Electoral College system was designed to ensure small states aren’t passed over by presidential campaigns, but in the process, it gives those often Republican-leaning states disproportionate control over presidential elections. It’s led to five cases in U.S. history where a candidate won the popular vote but lost the presidency, most recently in 2016 when Hillary Clinton lost to Donald Trump.

That’s why since 2006, some states have been working toward the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement to ensure that the candidate who wins the popular vote also wins the presidency. That two-decade effort could finally pay off, thanks to five states that flipped blue in the midterms.

How the midterms made it possible

For the compact to take effect, laws to join it must first be enacted by states whose combined electoral votes are enough to secure a presidential election. The 19 jurisdictions that have already passed laws pledging their votes to the compact (18 states and the District of Columbia) have a combined 222 electoral votes, still 48 shy of the 270 votes needed to win the presidency.

That’s where five newly blue states come in. Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania now have Democratic majorities in their state legislatures, matching their Democratic governors. Nevada’s voters flipped the state’s governorship from red to blue while maintaining a Democratic legislative majority.

Those states now have a Democratic trifecta, controlling both chambers of their state legislatures and their governorships, setting them up to join the compact if their lawmakers wish. If all five states did so, they’d push the compact past the 270-vote threshold, guaranteeing that the winner of the popular vote would win the presidency as early as the 2028 election.

Challenges to the compact

The compact wouldn’t technically get rid of the Electoral College, a change that would require amending the Constitution. Rather, it requires that all participating states pledge their electoral votes to whichever candidate wins the popular vote, even if that candidate didn’t get the majority of votes in their state.

The compact would likely face legal challenges. Even if the laws toward the compact are enacted in all five states, it may still need congressional approval under the Constitution’s Compact Clause, and still could face a possible presidential veto. The compact could also become the subject of a Supreme Court case, leaving it at the mercy of SCOTUS’s conservative majority.

Getting rid of the Electoral College is the favored position among voters, though support varies by political affiliation. As of 2024, 63% of American adults supported letting the popular vote decide the presidential election. That includes 80% of Democrats and 46% of Republicans. 

Still, whether states will actually take the leap and pledge their votes to the compact remains to be seen. Some key states have already blocked measures to join the compact in the past: In 2019, Nevada’s then-governor, Steve Sisolak, a Democrat, vetoed a bill to join, saying it could “diminish the role of smaller states like Nevada in national electoral contests.” In 2023, Michigan’s legislature did not pass a bill to join the compact, despite holding a Democratic trifecta at the time.

#10258. Wine and spirits could get cheaper after the midterms. Here’s why

Booze brands are hopeful that help is on the way for their industry—and they need it. Tariffs and declining drinking habits have weighed heavily on beverage companies over the last two years, but a change in control of Congress may signal near-term relief. 

The beverage market was apparently thirsty for good news. Stocks of some beer, wine, and liquor brands perked up after election results rolled in. Companies such as Diageo, the British beverage giant behind brands like Guinness and Smirnoff, and Brown-Forman, which makes spirits like Jack Daniel’s and Chambord, enjoyed a stock pop of more than 5% after Election Day. Anheuser-Busch; Molson Coors Beverage Co.; Boston Beer Co.; and Constellation Brands, which imports popular Mexican beer brands in the U.S., also experienced gains on Wednesday as the blue wave swept through.

Trump’s tariffs may have first turned international trade upside down last year, but their effects are still being felt. Last month, the U.S. charged ahead with a plan to ban almost $1 billion in imports from its northern neighbor, restricting the flow of Canadian dairy products, motorcycles, and alcoholic products. The ban was designed to punish Canada for pushing back with its own tariffs on American goods, but a 50% tariff already limited imports across many of those categories. Still, the full ban shows that Trump’s erratic trade wars rage on, even as American consumers shoulder much of the economic pain for those policies.

An existential threat

Alcoholic beverages make up the vast majority of the estimated $967 million in Canadian imports the ban is expected to impact, yet another symbolic blow for an industry already reeling from a perfect storm of market forces. Last year, Canadian stores yanked U.S. booze from their shelves after Trump announced a 25% tariff on almost all imports from Mexico and Canada. At the time, the Distilled Spirits Council, a beverage industry trade association, warned of “great harm” to U.S. companies and their workers in light of the tariffs, expressing further concern that Canada’s retaliation would worsen the stateside situation.

The trade wars amplify an already worrying forecast for the beverage industry, which is scrambling to adapt its business as alcohol consumption continues to plunge not only in the U.S. but also globally. In 2025, the share of American adults who said they drink alcohol dropped to 54%, according to polling from Gallup—lower by 1 percentage point than the previous record low reported in 1958 and a dramatic dip from 2022, when 67% of Americans said they were drinkers.

Drinking less, drinking differently

With drinking habits already drying up, the beverage industry is right to be worried that high costs are accelerating those trends.

In 2026, it wasn’t just expensive chocolate and unaffordable beef weighing down American shoppers. The price of beer, wine, and liquor soared too, putting a damper on drinking culture and straining sales for many booze-based businesses. In a recent survey of 1,000 Americans who drink, market research platform Zappi found that 65% of adults say they “pregame” by drinking at home before going out in order to save money on alcohol. This behavior, often thought of as a college-age ritual among cash-strapped students, is just one way consumers are grappling with the high price of drinks. 

“Pre-gaming is no longer a niche or age-specific behavior—it’s a mainstream occasion that brands need to design for deliberately,” Zappi suggested in its report. “Retail brands, particularly [ready-to-drink products], spirits, and hard seltzers, should be thinking about the ‘pre-game moment’ as a distinct occasion.”

The average price of a cocktail in the U.S. is now above $13—and much more in cities like New York where prices for everything are higher and drinking rituals run deep. Ordering a martini set consumers back an average of $18.63 in the U.S. this year, up 8% from a year ago, according to recent data from food-industry market research and consulting firm Technomic. Opting for a margarita would save you more than $8 compared with a martini, but those prices also crept up by roughly 2% on average in 2026 and as much as 33% in Alaska. 

The new premium on drinking is driving other market changes, too. Suntory Global Spirits CEO Greg Hughes told The Wall Street Journal that demand for its mini-bottles of liquor staples like Maker’s Mark and Jim Beam is surging as drinkers trim their alcohol budgets and order fewer drinks while going or dining out. “They’re trying to stretch the dollar by pregaming,” Hughes said. You can see that’s what’s growing.”

With Americans hurting from high costs, tariff relief is at the top of the menu for Democrats as they take control of Congress in January. “We’re paying a tremendous amount of money for this,” incoming Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed said in a podcast interview last week. He described ending the trade war with Canada as something Democrats “absolutely have to do immediately”—a priority he shares with the beverage industry.

“Getting American distilled spirits back on the shelves in Canada and securing the U.S. removal of the import ban on Canadian spirits remain top priorities for our industry, especially as we head into the crucial holiday season,” Chris Swonger, president and CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, told Fast Company. “A return to zero-for-zero tariffs on distilled spirits is a proven policy that has fostered economic growth for the hospitality industry, and we will continue to share that message with the administration and the new Congress.”

#10257. How to Get a YouTube API Key and Use the Data API (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You need a YouTube API key the moment your app has to read anything from YouTube: a video's length, its view count, a channel's latest uploads. Getting one takes about five minutes. Using it well takes a little longer, because YouTube changed how its quota works in June 2026, and plenty of guides still describe the old rules.

In this guide we'll get a key, lock it down and test it. Then we'll use it from Node.js for three real jobs: adding up the length of a playlist, listing a channel's videos without spending a search, and estimating what a video earned. Along the way we'll cover what the YouTube API costs (nothing), how the 2026 quota works, and the errors you're most likely to hit.

A YouTube API key identifies your project to the YouTube Data API v3. With just a key, you can read public data:

A key isn't enough for anything that touches someone's account. Uploading videos, editing playlists or reading private data needs OAuth 2.0, where the user signs in and grants your app access.

You'll need a Google account. The YouTube Data API is free, so there's nothing to pay for.

The restrictions matter more than they look. A key is just a string in a URL, and anyone who copies an unrestricted one can spend your daily quota for you. With an API restriction, the key is useless for other Google APIs. With an application restriction, it only works from your server or your site. Changes to restrictions can take up to five minutes to apply, so don't panic if a request fails straight after you save.

Before writing any code, check the key with a single request. This one asks for the first video ever uploaded to YouTube, and uses the fields parameter to trim the response down to four values:

That request cost 1 unit of your daily quota, which brings us to the question everyone asks.

Yes. There's no charge per request and no paid plan. Instead you get a daily quota, and since June 1, 2026 it's split into separate buckets:

Google's quota calculator lists the cost of every method. Quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time. Every request costs at least 1 unit, including requests that fail, so a retry loop around a broken call can use up a day's quota on its own.

If you've read older guides, search is the big change. A search used to cost 100 units out of the same 10,000, so 100 searches emptied your whole day. Uploads were worse still, at about 1,600 units each until December 2025. Now both have their own buckets, and the 10,000 units are left for everything else.

To give you a feel for what 10,000 units buys, here's what each example in this guide costs:

You can't pay for more. To go above the defaults, fill in the YouTube API Services Audit and Quota Extension Form, which is linked from Google's page on quota and compliance audits. YouTube first audits your project to check it follows the YouTube API Services Terms of Service, then someone from the API team gets back to you. Google doesn't give a timeline, so apply well before you need the extra quota.

Most projects never need to. The rest of this guide is about getting a lot done with very few units.

The examples need Node.js 20.6 or later, for the built-in fetch and the --env-file flag. There are no packages to install. Make a folder with a .env file in it:

Every example imports one small helper. It builds the URL, adds your key and turns API errors into readable messages:

Run any example with node --env-file=.env followed by the file name.

YouTube doesn't tell you how long a playlist is. To work it out, you need two methods:

Durations come back in ISO 8601 format. PT15M33S is 15 minutes 33 seconds, PT1H2M3S adds an hour, and a stream longer than a day looks like P1DT2H3M4S. The toSeconds() function below handles all three.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Full Courses in One Video playlist:

That's 184 hours of courses for 4 units of quota. Private and deleted videos still show up in a playlist's items, but videos.list doesn't return them, which is why the script prints "52 of 52 videos available". On a playlist with removed videos, the two numbers will differ.

This is the core of the free YouTube playlist length calculator I built on createthat.ai. The live version adds a target time box that works out the speed you need to finish by a deadline, and it accepts channel, video and Shorts links as well as playlists.

The obvious way to find a channel's videos is to search for them. Don't: search is now capped at 100 calls a day, and it isn't built to list everything a channel has posted. Every channel has an uploads playlist instead, and you can reach it in two cheap calls:

Two units, and none of your 100 daily searches. To get every upload rather than the newest five, page through the playlist with the same pageToken loop as Example 1.

videos.list with part=statistics returns a video's view, like and comment counts. Dislike counts have been private since December 2021 and favoriteCount is always 0, so don't build anything on those. The script also copes with a missing like or comment count, which you'll see on some videos.

This time the fields parameter trims the response to the values we use. That makes the response smaller, but it doesn't change the cost: the call is 1 unit either way.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Learn Python full course, one of the most-watched videos in that playlist:

Treat the last line as a rough range, not an answer. The Data API doesn't share anyone's revenue, so any estimate is views multiplied by an RPM: what a creator keeps per 1,000 views. RPM moves a lot with the topic and where the viewers live, and the estimate assumes the video shows ads, which not every channel does.

And sometimes you don't need an API at all. When I built a font tester, I needed a list of Google Fonts. The Google Fonts Developer API would have meant a key and a call on every visit, for a list that barely changes. Instead I generated a file of the 500 most popular fonts once, from Google's public font metadata, and the page loads it like any other file. No key, no quota and nothing to fail.

When a call fails, the response's error.message and error.details[0].reason tell you why. These are the ones you'll see most:

For the invalid key error, the full response looks like this:

Yes. Creating a key and calling the YouTube Data API costs nothing. You're limited by the daily quota instead, and there's no paid tier: more quota comes through an audit.

In the Google Cloud console, select your project and go to APIs & Services > Credentials. Your keys are listed under API keys, with a Show key option next to each one.

It works, but anyone can read the key from your page. If you do it, restrict the key to your website and to the YouTube Data API v3. A small server route that calls the API for you is safer, and it gives you somewhere to cache results.

By default, 100 searches, 100 uploads and 10,000 units for everything else. Most reads cost 1 unit and videos.list takes 50 IDs per call, so that's enough for the details of up to 500,000 videos a day.

Getting a YouTube API key is the easy part: one project, one API to enable, one key and two restrictions. The 2026 quota is generous if you work with it:

All three examples together cost 7 units, out of 10,000. From here, try commentThreads.list to pull a video's comments 100 at a time, or extend Example 2 to page through a channel's entire upload history and add it all up with the code from Example 1.

Open source tool is available for Windows, Linux, and macOS.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microsoft VP Scott Hanselman has revealed a new open-source GitHub project called gputaskman. The name neatly encapsulates the headline role of this tool, a GPU-focused task manager, but its scope might be broader than you expect. This new tool for Windows, Linux, and macOS can show per-process GPU usage, VRAM consumption, active runtimes, and many more stats. It also breaks out AI/LLM task-specific information.

There's a lot going on in my GPU. I'm making a GPU Taskman to get insights to where my GPU memory is going. PRs welcome https://t.co/6FwKqnFWDWNovember 3, 2026

On social media, Hanselman snappily makes clear the technical itch that gputaskman was designed to scratch. “There's a lot going on in my GPU,” wrote the prominent public face of Microsoft's developer ecosystem. “I'm making a GPU Taskman to get insights to where my GPU memory is going.”

There are several example screenshots of GPU Taskman in use by the Microsoft VP. They clearly show the kinds of data that are presented in the terminal-like display that pops up in the tool. Hanselman’s tweet shows that the most VRAM-hungry app on his RTX 4080S system is the desktop windows manager. That is selected in the list, and more details are shown for this task at the bottom of the window. Also, we see AI/LLM apps consuming VRAM, and a few Windows staples.

In a GitHub-embedded image, we see what details are broken out when the llama-server.exe app is selected in the list. The bottom of the window breakdown reveals that Qwen3-0.6B is being used, and there’s a breakdown of its weights, the KV cache, the number of parameters, and more. Very informative.

As the Microsoft developer has made portable Windows downloads of the latest v0.3.0 release of gputaskman, I couldn’t resist giving it a spin. Upon launch, I found that no tasks were using the discrete GPU in my laptop… so I fired up ye olde Unigine Valley GPU benchmark to stir the RTX 4060 from its slumber. I note the live-streaming charts showing GPU load, VRAM use, temperature, and so on are more prominent in my screenshot than in Hanselman’s examples. Perhaps he screen-shotted a previous version of the tool.

There’s a lot more information about gputaskman, its inner workings, and even its source code, on the linked GitHub repository. Hanselman is sharing his “experimental software” tool under the permissive MIT license. Finally, in social media comments, he hints that expanded GPU monitoring capabilities could be coming to Windows as standard.
