#10146. Fitbit Sense & Versa losing 3rd-party watch faces this month, existing downloads remain

Google announced today that Fitbit Sense and Versa smartwatches will soon lose the ability to “install or update third-party apps and clocks.”

This change to the Fitbit App Gallery applies to the Versa, Versa 2, Versa 3, Versa 4, Sense, and Sense 2.

Existing “third-party apps or clock faces installed on your Fitbit device” will remain available, but you can no longer download new ones (or update them) starting November 28. As such, “if you choose to delete an app or clock face, or factory reset your device, you will no longer be able to re-install it.”

Instead, the Fitbit App Gallery will “exclusively feature apps and clock faces created by Fitbit and Google.”

The November 28 deadline also applies to third-party developers. Google will “no longer support uploading new apps and clock faces or updating existing ones.”

Google winding down Fitbit OS for smartwatches is not particularly surprising as the company has been all-in on Wear OS and the Pixel Watch. That said, the Sense 2 and Versa 4 should probably no longer be on sale.

#10144. Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

We tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the new text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:

One help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:

Each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

LangSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation says you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

Langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation shows only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

Errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:

The rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per new set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

#10143. Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).

For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. Both engines already run on TPU through JAX-based backends, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.

So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.

Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.

Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem.

TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a tpu device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via torch.compile using XLA, and collectives go through torch.distributed.

Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager, API server and so forth, with TPU implementations underneath.

Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in both engines, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace.

Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.

Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier.

Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency.

Both engines use TPU Sync for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache.

Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.

Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.

We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first:

This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios.

Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas megakernel for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary AgentX submission for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation.

To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to the vLLM engine.

As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours!

Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations.

vLLM-JAX and SGLang-JAX remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt.

#10134. Samsung Galaxy S27 series camera specs leak, and they’re disappointing

New leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.

SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.

The base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at new hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.

Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a new 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing users of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.

Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but shows the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. We’re assuming that’s a typo seeing as the post mentions the Pro as using the Samsung S5KJN3 or the Sony IMX855 earlier on, but regardless, the Pro only gets 3x optical zoom to the Ultra’s 5x.

Some of these specs have been mentioned by other sources such as GalaxyClub and leaker Ice Universe, but this is the most complete picture of the S27’s camera plans we’ve seen to date.

Personally, I’m very “whelmed” on this one. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for new ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. #10133. Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer

Model Explorer goes beyond high-level model graphs. See how Arm plugs in custom compiler IRs, verifies NPU delegation side-by-side, and maps cycle-level profiling traces directly onto your execution graph.

Machine learning models run locally on a wide range of hardware, from low-power edge devices to gaming graphics and physical AI systems. Running models efficiently on these targets requires compilation steps such as quantization, graph lowering, operator fusion, and hardware delegation.

Arm used Google AI Edge Model Explorer to give developers visibility into these pipelines. With Model Explorer's hierarchical graph visualization and plugin architecture, Arm built several open-source adapters that make edge model transformations easier to inspect.

When deploying a model to edge hardware, a framework change or operator constraint can alter the exported execution graph. Engineers often need to answer three questions:

Answering these questions by reading raw flatbuffers or text logs takes time, especially for large language models (LLMs) and neural networks. Arm needed a visual tool to inspect Arm-specific intermediate representations and hardware profiling traces.

To address these deployment challenges, Arm developed custom adapters for Google AI Edge Model Explorer to support several model formats (i.e., TOSA, VGF, and PTE), establishing a comprehensive visual workflow for on-device optimization. Using these extensions, engineering teams can validate exported pipelines, verify accelerator delegation, and pinpoint cycle-level performance bottlenecks directly on the model graph:

Arm engineers used Model Explorer to validate a PyTorch-trained Neural Super Sampling (NSS) model exported through the ExecuTorch Arm backend as a VGF file for Vulkan ML Extensions. While inspecting the VGF graph, the team found unintended TRANSPOSE operators introduced by a change in the ExecuTorch Arm backend.

Model Explorer enables users to inspect individual nodes of the model graph, such as the rescale operator depicted below, which displays the operator's attributes and SPIR-V tensor connections. This functionality assisted the Arm team in identifying and resolving the regression without requiring manual analysis of raw log files.

To optimize vision models for accelerators like the Arm Ethos-U85 NPU, Arm engineers used Model Explorer's split-pane view to compare CPU and NPU-delegated graphs side-by-side for a Ultralytics YOLO model.

The split-pane view showed the structural difference: the CPU graph displays each individual layer, while the NPU graph groups the network into a single EthosUBackend block between quantize and dequantize nodes. For partially supported models in LiteRT or ExecuTorch, this view helps identify un-delegated operators and split subgraphs.

To find latency bottlenecks on the Ethos-U NPU, Arm ran their model on their Fixed Virtual Platform (FVP) simulator and used Model Explorer's node data plugin to overlay cycle-accurate execution traces onto the graph. Color-coded heatmaps showed that a single TRANSPOSE node was the main latency bottleneck.

You can use Google AI Edge Model Explorer along with Arm's open-source adapters today to inspect and optimize your own on-device models locally via PyPI or GitHub.

#10132. Technical Aspects of AI-Generated Video Assets for Web Design

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how quickly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially important for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

Trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract users or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally important. Smaller screens, limited data plans, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

#10122. Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

To compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

QuillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

Custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

Pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the plans page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid plans also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

Variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

There isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

#10116. Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon

Edge AI complements the cloud to bring the best AI experiences. These rely on a continuous flow of context and intelligence across both, working as a model cascade where information is captured and processed in the right place at the right time. Ultra-low-power models on the edge can continuously sense and respond in real time, while seamlessly handing off to larger on-device or cloud models when deeper reasoning is needed.

Still, building for the edge is much harder than it should be. While cloud infrastructure has converged around a few standard software stacks, the edge is split across hundreds of proprietary chip architectures and incompatible toolchains. For ML developers, this creates a heavy fragmentation tax, where you end up rewriting kernels, re-quantizing models, and debugging vendor-specific compilers for every chip you target.

Last year, Google Research introduced Coral NPU with a simple idea: an open hardware and software standard is the only way to unify the edge and unlock developer productivity and portability. Our standards based, ML-first RISC-V architecture paired with a reliable open-source toolchain gives developers confidence that their models will compile and run, letting teams optimize a model once and deploy it across different SoC vendors, devices, and power envelopes.

Today, we are reaching three major milestones in the Coral effort:

Fixing fragmentation at the edge takes more than publishing an instruction set. Historically, many edge accelerators were designed to hit high peak-compute numbers on spec sheets, leaving compiler teams to figure out software support later. In practice, unsupported neural network layers fall back to a general-purpose CPU, which can hurt latency and drain the battery.

We designed the Coral NPU architecture and its compiler together from the start. Instead of chasing peak metrics, our focus is on energy-viable compute: helping to deliver the right performance at the right power envelope for your application.

Over the past year, we released the first three milestones of the 32-bit Coral NPU design: a C-programmable RISC-V scalar frontend for control flow (Milestone 1), an RVV v1.0 vector co-processor for SIMD operations (Milestone 2), and a tightly coupled memory subsystem with floating point support (Milestone 3). With this month's release of the Matrix Execution Unit (Milestone 4), the 32-bit architecture is complete.

Scalar and vector units are great for general control logic and signal processing, but modern ML workloads—from vision encoders to transformer attention layers—spend most of their time on 2D matrix-matrix (GEMM) and matrix-vector (GEMV) multiplication. Running 2D matrix math on a 1D vector engine forces the chip to repeatedly load weights and activations from memory, which can mean spending more energy moving data than doing math.

Our Matrix Execution Unit leverages the RISC-V VME specification (formally part of the Zvt family) to address this need and uses a dedicated outer-product multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine. Because an outer-product engine computes a full 2D tile of operations in a single cycle (256 MACs per cycle), it reuses weights and activations directly inside local registers. This brings quadratic throughput scaling to the core, configurable for up to 1 TOPS.

Having a dedicated matrix engine in a sub-10 mW envelope changes what developers can build on a small battery. Rather than stopping at simple keyword spotting or basic motion detection, devices can run continuous, multimodal workloads, including compact transformer models like Gemma, real-time voice translation on wearables, spatial audio filtering on hearables, and low-latency visual perception on robots.

To help silicon teams bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub.

To make the hardware easy to target without writing custom assembly, we are also releasing the v1.0 foundation of our open-source MLIR/IREE compiler toolchain.

With this stack, you can bring models from JAX, PyTorch, or TensorFlow through standard representations like StableHLO and TOSA. The compiler partitions workloads between the host CPU and the Coral NPU core, handles operator fusion, tiles matrices to fit local SRAM and matrix accumulators, and progressively lowers workloads directly to Coral NPU scalar, RVV v1.0 vector, and VME matrix instructions. Alongside our open-source MPACT simulator and reference FPGA design, hardware and software teams can benchmark models and tune silicon configurations before a chip ever goes to fabrication.

Turning an open standard into commercial silicon takes collaboration across the entire semiconductor value chain. To help silicon partners bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub, and we are partnering with VeriSilicon on the design implementation and verification (DV) to ensure turnkey readiness for silicon tape-outs. We are also working with GlobalFoundries on their 12LP+ FinFET process - accelerating core timing by 70%, and reducing standard-cell area by up to 15% across RTL iterations, with ongoing evaluation of 12LP+ ultra low-power libraries for the Matrix Execution Unit.

On the commercial silicon side, our collaboration with Synaptics shows how quickly this open standard translates into real hardware across very different power budgets without splitting the software experience.

At Synaptics Tech Day (October 20, 2026), Synaptics is launching three commercial silicon and hardware products built on Coral NPU technology and supported by the open IREE/MLIR toolchain:

Because both product families build on the same architecture and compiler foundation, ML teams can optimize a model once and deploy it to a milliwatt-class wearable (Coralboard SR) or a 1 TOPS board (Coralboard SL) using the same workflow. Developed in collaboration with hardware and System-on-Module partner Grinn, the Coralboard lineup also gives teams a direct path from devkit prototyping to commercial production hardware.

With our 32-bit architecture and v1.0 compiler stack in place, we are already working on the next phase of the roadmap, including a 64-bit Coral NPU architecture and CHERI support for security.

Whether you are designing a custom edge SoC, working on ML compilers, or deploying models to wearables and robotics, Coral NPU can help give you an open path from model to silicon. Here is where you can get started:

We would like to thank the core contributors and leadership team for this work, particularly Billy Rutledge, Ben Laurie, Derek Chow, Shaked Flur, Alex Van Damme, Bilal Khan, David Gao, Gregory Kielian, Julian Mullings-Black, Khaled Talukder, Lun Dong, Matthew Wilson, Michael Hoang, Murali Vijayaraghavan, Naveen Dodda, Roman Lewkow, Stefan Hall, Tor Jeremiassen, Yenkai Wang, Manya Dasari, Akib Uddin, Divya Pandya, Steve He, Preeti Singh, Anthony Phalen, Hans Rempel, Esmeralda Cardenas, Isha Mishra, Katy Zima, Resham Parikh, Hannah Bayer Rushing, Taylor Montgomery, Kai Yick, Srikanth Muroor, Cindy Liu, Bangfei Pan, Alec Go, Geoff Stirling, Robin Dua, Gaurav Arora, Steve Goldberg, Francesco Visin, Gus Martins, Ian Ballantyne, Kat Black, Ravin Kumar, Tris Warkentin, Avinatan Hassidim, Jay Yagnik, Katherine Chou, Shahram Izadi, and Yossi Matias.

#10115. From User Feedback to a Better Prompt: 4 Tools Tested in TypeScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs shows it. The request returns 200, the JSON is valid, and no exception fires. Usually the user is the only one who notices. A thumbs-down button records that moment, on the exact trace that went wrong, while the user still remembers why.

That button is easy to add. The hard part is what comes after: turning the thumbs-down into a reviewed test case, a judge score, and a better prompt.

We ran that loop in TypeScript in four tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. All four handled the first four steps, which are user feedback, reviewer comments, a dataset and an LLM judge. Only AcruxCore rewrote the prompt from TypeScript. On 15 support tickets that no tool had seen, the rewritten prompt routed 13 correctly, against 7 for the original.

Our test app is a support-ticket router. It reads a ticket and returns JSON with a category (account, billing, bug or feature_request) and a priority (P0, P1 or P2). The first version of the prompt describes only the output format:

The support team has a policy that this prompt never states. Sign-in problems are always account. A customer who can't use the product at all is P0. Any billing error is P1, even when the customer says there is no rush. Feature requests are P2, however angry the customer sounds.

Without that policy, the model guesses priority from the customer's tone. Here are three real replies from the first version:

Every reply is valid JSON, so no schema check catches the mistake. A person has to read the reply and say it is wrong. The loop in this article takes that judgement and turns it into a better prompt.

All four tools cover evaluation. We compared the self-hosted ones on tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent, and on prompt registries in Prompt Management in TypeScript. For a broader comparison of self-hosted options, see this LangSmith alternatives roundup. This article covers the feedback loop only.

We wrote 30 tickets. Fifteen are the "production traffic" that each tool's app processed. The other 15 are a holdout set. No tool saw them, and we used them only for the final before-and-after check.

Each tool ran the same sequence from one TypeScript script:

The reviewer comments follow one template, so the wording is identical in every tool:

The comments name one rule each. The full policy appears nowhere in the data any tool received.

The app model isn't fully deterministic at temperature 0. Each tool's run got between 6 and 8 of the 15 traffic tickets right, so the tools received 7 to 9 thumbs-down each. The holdout check below repeats every measurement three times.

All four tools accept feedback on a trace from TypeScript. They differ in how a second person, the reviewer, adds the correct answer.

LangSmith stores both as feedback on a run. The thumbs-down runs go into an annotation queue, where a reviewer adds feedback with a comment:

Langfuse stores both as scores. An annotation queue needs a score config first:

Phoenix stores both as span annotations. The reviewer's comment goes in explanation:

Phoenix stores spans asynchronously. Our first run annotated a span before Phoenix had stored it, and the API returned a 404. The script now waits until all 15 spans are visible.

AcruxCore stores both as feedback rows on the trace. The source field separates the end user from the reviewer:

This is the first step where the code differs a lot. Each tool can make a dataset, but only one builds it from feedback in one call.

In LangSmith, a run query finds the thumbs-down runs. Then createExamples copies them into a dataset. You decide where the reviewer's comment goes. We put it in the reference output:

LangSmith can also do this without code. An automation rule in the UI can add runs that match a filter to a dataset.

In Langfuse, the scores API finds the thumbs-down traces. Two details cost us a run each. A boolean score is filtered with value: "false", not 0. And the trace ID is returned only when you ask for the subject field group:

In Phoenix, getSpans can't filter by annotation. So the script lists the app's spans, reads their annotations, and keeps the ones with a thumbs-down. Then createDataset takes the examples. We kept the source span ID in the metadata.

In AcruxCore, buildFromFeedback takes the reviewer's feedback IDs. Each comment becomes that example's grading criteria, and the input comes from the variables captured on the trace:

Each tool scored the first version of the prompt on its own dataset. The judge read the reviewer's comment and the router's reply, and returned 1 for a match and 0 for a mismatch.

LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix each have an experiment runner that takes your evaluator function, and we gave all three the same judge prompt. AcruxCore grades with its built-in judge inside the optimize run. All four used the same judge model.

The first version fails almost every reviewed case. That is expected, because these are the cases users marked wrong. A score of 1 means the app model got that case right on the second call, or the judge accepted a wrong reply. We didn't check which.

The judge can also run without your code. Besides the in-code evaluator we used, Langfuse has a managed LLM-as-a-judge that runs on production traces and on experiments, with your own judge prompt. LangSmith has online evaluators, which you set up in its UI, for the same job.

An optimizer reads the failing cases and the reviewer comments, writes new versions of the prompt, and scores each one with the judge. This is the step that turns feedback into a better prompt, and it's where the four tools differ most.

LangSmith's API reference lists an optimize prompt job (POST /api/v1/repos/optimize-job). It takes a prompt name, a dataset name, evaluator IDs and an algorithm, promptim or demo. No method in the TypeScript SDK wraps it, so we called it with fetch. We gave it a code evaluator that checks the reply against the reviewer's correct answer.

The job was accepted and reported successful about ten seconds later. It ran no experiment on the dataset. With auto_commit set to true, it added no new commit to the prompt. We found no guide for this endpoint, so we may have configured it wrongly, but the job record and its logs gave no error to act on.

LangSmith's documented route to prompt optimization is promptim, which its README calls an experimental library. It is a Python package with a CLI, and it can add a human review step through LangSmith annotation queues.

Langfuse has no optimizer. Its blog shows a workflow with Claude Code agent skills that reads Langfuse data and edits the prompt. That workflow runs in a coding agent, not in your app's code.

Phoenix's Optimize Prompts Automatically tutorial uses Arize's prompt-learning package, which you clone from GitHub and install with pip. The Phoenix TypeScript client has no optimizer export, and the tutorial runs outside Phoenix. Arize's commercial platform, Arize AX, has prompt optimization built in.

For Python teams, there are more options: Opik's Agent Optimizer and DSPy both rewrite prompts from a dataset and a metric. This article covers TypeScript.

Its optimize run takes the dataset and drafts three rewrites of the production prompt. It runs each rewrite and the current production version on every example, and the judge grades all of them:

The three rewrites tied, so we took candidate A. Its rationale: "Added explicit priority rules for each category and clarified that access-blocking issues are P0, billing errors are P1, and feature requests are P2, overriding tone/urgency." The Improve a prompt from feedback guide covers the dashboard version of this step.

A rewrite that passes the cases it was built from can still fail on new tickets. So we ran both prompts on the 15 holdout tickets, three times each, outside every tool. The script calls the model directly and checks the category and the priority against the expected answer. No judge is involved.

Both come from one line in the rewrite: "P1 for bugs without workaround." That rule isn't in the team's policy, and no reviewer wrote it. The optimizer made it up to explain the examples it had. There was also no outage in the traffic set's thumbs-down cases, because the first version routed that one correctly. So no comment ever said that a full outage is P0.

The optimizer learns only from what users marked wrong. Anything they never marked stays a guess, and the rationale won't tell you which rules are guesses. Read the rewritten prompt before you promote it.

In LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix, shipping a new version is a tag or label move. We showed those calls in the prompt-management article. Here there was no rewrite to ship, so the step didn't apply.

In AcruxCore, promotion commits the candidate as a new prompt version and moves the production alias to it. Nothing else moves:

The app renders production on every call, so the next ticket used version 2 without a deploy.

Use LangSmith if your team already works in it and writes Python. Feedback, queues, datasets and experiments all work from TypeScript, and promptim covers optimization from Python.

Use Langfuse if you want a managed judge that runs on live traces with your own prompt. Plan to write the dataset glue code and the rewrite step yourself.

Use Phoenix if you already trace with OpenTelemetry and annotate spans. Plan to move to Python, or to Arize AX, for optimization.

Use AcruxCore if you want all six steps from TypeScript in one tool, including the rewrite. Keep a human on the promote button.
